At Intern level you'll learn the language of drawing, scale and how to draw a plan.
A day in the life of an architect
The day usually starts with emails and drawings. Plans, sections and 3D models are worked on at the computer.
You listen to what the client wants: how many rooms, what budget, what kind of life. A good architect is first a good listener.
The plot where the building will go is seen in person: where the sun comes from, where the view is, how close the neighbouring buildings are, whether the land slopes.
Every building has rules it must follow: the zoning plan, regulations, earthquake and fire rules. The architect looks for the best design within these rules.
During construction the architect visits the site and checks that what's on the drawings is being built correctly.
How do you become an architect?
In Türkiye you study a 4-year architecture degree at university. An architect practising independently must be registered with the Chamber of Architects. This game is preparation for that path.
Today is your trial day at an architecture office. The senior architect has brought you to your first meeting.
Client: "Draw us a house." What do you do first?
I listen and ask how many people will live there, what they need and what their budget is
Design starts with questions. A house drawn without knowing the needs suits no one.
I immediately draw the most beautiful house on paper
It could be a beautiful but useless house. Learn the needs first.
I show them a house I liked online
Every family and every plot is different; a ready-made house doesn't fit everywhere.
Senior architect: "We're going to the plot. What do you note down?"
The direction of the sun, the view, the slope and the neighbouring buildings
These decide where the rooms will go.
I just take photos of the plot
Photos help, but you need direction and measurement information.
Nothing, we'll sort it out at the office
A plot not seen in person brings surprises.
Client: "Let's build over the whole plot, I don't want a garden."
I explain that we need to check, under the zoning rules, how much of the plot the building can cover
On every plot, the area a building may cover and its distance from the boundaries are set by rules.
I say "Okay" and draw it that way
A project that breaks the rules isn't approved, and the client loses out.
Explaining the rules honestly is the architect's job.
There are no right or wrong answers. Choose the one closest to you.
Drawing at a computer for hours?
I could get used to it
Looking at a building and wondering how it was built?
Redrawing when your idea isn't liked?

What does the "±0.00" mark on a plan show?
The building's zero level, the reference for all heights
A level (kot) is a point's height relative to zero. +3.00 means 3 m above zero, −2.80 means 2.80 m below.
Why are cut walls drawn with thick lines on a plan?
Cut elements are drawn thickest and distant visible lines thin, so the drawing reads easily
A thick line always means concrete
Line weight tells depth: cut is thick, visible is thin, hidden is dashed.
What's in the title block (antet) in the corner of a sheet?
Project name, drawing name, scale, date, sheet number, drawn by and approved by
The title block is the sheet's ID; on site, workers know which drawing they're reading from it.
You changed a drawing. What goes on the sheet?
A revision number, its date and what changed
The old sheet is thrown away with no record
Working from an old drawing on site leads to costly mistakes. A revision record makes sure everyone uses the latest one.
In a dimension chain the parts don't add up to the overall dimension. What do you do?
Find where the error is, fix it and tell the architect in charge
The builders will sort it out on site

A dimension that doesn't add up means a wall built in the wrong place. Always check that dimensions add up.
Cut thick, visible thin, hidden dashed.
The title block is the sheet's ID.

The ratio of the building's ground footprint to the plot
TAKS (building coverage ratio): footprint area ÷ plot area.
The plot is 500 m², TAKS 0.30. At most how many m² can the building cover on the ground?
What does KAKS (floor area ratio) show?
The ratio of total floor area to plot area
KAKS (floor area ratio): area of all floors ÷ plot area.
The plot is 500 m², KAKS 1.20. At most how many m² of total floor area can be built?
Unless the plan says otherwise, what is the minimum side setback for a detached building, in metres?
The general rule is 3 m; for buildings over 4 storeys it increases by 0.50 m for each extra storey.
Unless the plan says otherwise, what is the front setback usually, in metres?
The general rule is 5 m; the zoning plan may set a different value.
TAKS × plot = the largest possible footprint.
KAKS × plot = the largest possible total floor area.

Place the rooms by the sun
In Türkiye the south façade gets the most sun throughout the day. Place each space on the façade that usually suits it best.
The place where most time is spent goes on the façade that gets the most sun.
It's used all day; it needs sun and light.
It faces south to collect the sun.
It's used briefly; it leaves the sunny façade to living spaces.
Wet rooms used briefly can go on the north side.
North light is soft and steady all day; painters love it.
It faces south for sunbathing in winter.
North: pantry, stairs, wet rooms, studio.
The west façade gets very hot on summer afternoons; think about shading.
These are general principles; the view and climate also affect the decision.
You're an architect now. You're designing a two-storey house for a family.
Client: "The living room should be on the north, the view is there."
I suggest a big window facing the view and a corner that gets light from the south
Good design combines both wishes: the view and the sun.
I say "That's the rule, the living room goes on the south"
The sun principle is a recommendation, not a rule; the client's wish matters.
I put it on the north without question; light doesn't matter
A dark living room becomes a complaint over time; explain the options.
Client: "The budget isn't enough, but I won't give up anything."
We rank the priorities together and set aside what can be added later
The budget is real; the architect offers honest options.

What's the common comfort rule for stairs?
The higher the riser, the better
The formula is based on the human stride. For exact limits, always check the current regulations for each project.
The riser is 17 cm. Using 2 × riser + tread = 62 cm, how deep is the tread?
Floor-to-floor height is 306 cm. With 17 cm risers, how many risers do you need?
306 ÷ 17 = 18 risers. All risers must be equal; one odd step makes people trip.
What's the usual height of a kitchen counter?
It's the height for working standing up without bending; a dining table is about 75 cm because you sit at it.
What matters when designing for a wheelchair user?
Wide doors, level thresholds, turning space and ramps
The measurements for accessible design are set out in TS 9111; good design is easier for everyone.
Check the regulations for exact limits.
You're working on an apartment building. If there's a fire, everyone must be able to get out safely.
Client: "Let's make the staircase narrower so the flats are bigger."

Explain that escape route widths are set by regulations and suggest gaining space elsewhere
Listen to the client but don't compromise safety; look for the solution elsewhere.

Senior architect: "What kind of doors should the stairwell have?"
An enclosed, protected stair stays a safe escape route as long as smoke can't get in.

The door's fire resistance time is set by the regulations.
Which way should an escape door open?
In a panic the crowd presses against the door; an inward door can't be opened.
In the direction of escape, outward
A door opening in the direction of escape opens at a push.
A sliding door on an escape route can jam in a panic.
Client: "In a fire everyone takes the lift down; we don't need stairs."
In a fire the power can fail and the lift shaft can fill with smoke.
Explain that ordinary lifts aren't used for escape in a fire and stairs are mandatory
That's why lifts carry the sign "Do not use in case of fire".
We'll put in two lifts; that'll do
No number of lifts replaces the stairs.
Residents want to keep bikes and cupboards on the stair landings.
Anything on an escape route is an obstacle in smoke and extra fuel for the fire.
Say escape routes must stay clear and suggest a separate storage area in the building

The rule isn't about the type of item; the route must stay clear.
Stairs are enclosed, with self-closing doors.
Escape doors open outward; lifts aren't used.
